title: What Is Environmental History?
description: Origins of the field, first vs second nature, and the historians who built it

concepts.title: A Field Born in the 1970s
concepts.contentHtml:
Environmental history studies the reciprocal relationship between humans and the rest of nature across time. It treats climate, soil, microbes, animals, forests, and rivers as historical actors rather than mere backdrop. The field crystallised in the United States in the 1970s, riding the wake of Silent Spring (1962), Earth Day (1970), and a growing scholarly suspicion that traditional history had treated the non-human world as a stage set.

Three figures anchor its founding generation. Donald Worster's Dust Bowl (1979) showed how capitalism plus drought plus plough produced one of the twentieth century's most haunting ecological disasters. Alfred Crosby's The Columbian Exchange (1972) reframed 1492 as a biological event. William Cronon's Changes in the Land (1983) showed how New England's ecosystems were transformed by colonial property regimes long before factories appeared.

The field has since become global. Indian scholars (Ramachandra Guha, Madhav Gadgil), Latin Americanists (Shawn Miller, Stuart McCook), and African historians (William Beinart) have decentred its US origin and reshaped it as a planetary discipline.

concepts.title: First Nature, Second Nature
concepts.contentHtml:
Cronon's later book Nature's Metropolis (1991) introduced a distinction borrowed from Hegel and reworked for ecology. First nature is the world as it existed before human intervention — prairies, virgin forests, free-flowing rivers. Second nature is the human-built environment that overlays it: railways, fields, cities, drainage systems. We almost never encounter first nature directly anymore; what we call "nature" is usually second nature mistaken for the original.

The distinction destabilises the romantic notion of pristine wilderness. The Amazon rainforest the Spaniards saw in 1500 was already shaped by millennia of indigenous burning, fish-weir building, and terra preta soil engineering. Yellowstone before the Park Service was Crow, Bannock, and Shoshone land managed with fire. There is no untouched baseline; only differently touched landscapes.

This insight cuts two ways. It rebuts the conservationist fantasy of restoring "pristine" ecosystems (pristine when?). And it rebuts the despairing claim that human influence is wholly recent — humans have been remaking ecosystems since the Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.

concepts.title: McNeill and the Global Turn
concepts.contentHtml:
John R. McNeill's Something New Under the Sun (2000) is the field's most-cited synthesis of the twentieth century. McNeill's argument: humans of the 1900s did more to alter the biosphere than all previous generations combined. Atmospheric CO₂, nitrogen flux, fish biomass, freshwater extraction, soil erosion — every metric inflects sharply upward after 1945.

McNeill follows up with The Great Acceleration (2014, with Peter Engelke), tracing what Earth-system scientists call the post-1950 inflection: human activity becomes the dominant force restructuring planetary processes. His Mosquito Empires (2010) inverts the lens, showing how yellow fever and malaria — not just navies — decided the fate of Caribbean colonialism, with disease ecology actively making and unmaking empires.

The McNeillian vision treats environmental history as a planetary science with archives. Pollen cores, ice cores, tree rings, and historical accounts are all evidence. The historian must learn to read both Latin chronicles and stable isotope ratios. The field's methodological openness is its greatest strength and its hardest pedagogical demand.

title: The Anthropocene Debate
description: Crutzen 2000, competing start dates, and the ICS rejection

concepts.title: Crutzen, Stoermer, and a Word
concepts.contentHtml:
In February 2000, atmospheric chemist Paul Crutzen reportedly interrupted a conference in Cuernavaca, Mexico to declare: "We are no longer in the Holocene. We are in the Anthropocene." Later that year, with biologist Eugene Stoermer, he published a short note in the IGBP newsletter formally proposing the term. The 2002 Nature piece "Geology of Mankind" took the idea mainstream.

The proposal was simple. Holocene-era stratigraphic baselines no longer described Earth's behaviour. Atmospheric composition, sediment flux, biotic distributions, and climatic forcing had all been knocked off their Holocene tracks by human activity. A new epoch should be named.

What Crutzen did not specify was when the Anthropocene began. He gestured toward the late eighteenth century and James Watt's steam engine (1784) — but acknowledged this was provisional. The starting-date question turned out to be the most contentious dimension of the entire debate, and remains unresolved a quarter-century later.

concepts.title: Three Candidate Start Dates
concepts.contentHtml:
Three start dates dominate the Anthropocene literature, each carrying a different political argument.

1610 — the Orbis Spike. Lewis and Maslin (Nature, 2015) propose 1610, the lowest point of a CO₂ dip recorded in Antarctic ice cores. They link it to the death of perhaps 50 million indigenous Americans after 1492, whose abandoned fields reforested and drew down atmospheric carbon. The Anthropocene begins as a stratigraphic record of genocide.

~1800 — the Industrial Onset. Crutzen's original choice. Coal-burning, fossil carbon emissions, and the steam engine define a clear shift in atmospheric chemistry. This locates blame squarely on industrial capitalism and its European originators.

1950 — the Great Acceleration. Will Steffen and the IGBP team show that nearly every Earth-system metric (CO₂, methane, surface temperature, marine fisheries, dam-building, fertiliser use) bends sharply upward around 1950. This is also when bomb-test radionuclides leave a globally synchronous stratigraphic marker — the so-called "bomb spike" — useful for ICS-style golden-spike definition.

concepts.title: The ICS Vote and What Came After
concepts.contentHtml:
The International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) is the body that formally names geological epochs. Its Anthropocene Working Group (AWG), chaired by Jan Zalasiewicz, spent fifteen years building the case for a 1950s start date with a Golden Spike at Crawford Lake, Ontario, where varved sediments preserve the bomb spike, fly ash, and microplastic markers.

In March 2024, the ICS Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted down the Anthropocene proposal. Procedural disputes followed, but the formal verdict is clear: as of 2026, we still officially live in the Holocene's Meghalayan stage. The reasons cited included the Anthropocene's brevity (an epoch defined by 70 years), the difficulty of synchronising multiple proposed markers, and concern that elevating Anthropocene to a stratigraphic unit conflated geology with politics.

The rejection has barely slowed the term's spread. Anthropologists, historians, philosophers (Chakrabarty, Latour, Haraway) and Earth scientists continue to use it as a heuristic for the human-dominated planet, regardless of stratigraphic officialdom. The label has escaped its taxonomic cage.

title: Pre-Modern Environmental Disasters
description: Salinization, lead, drought, and the trouble with Easter Island

concepts.title: Mesopotamia: When Salt Killed Civilisations
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sumerian heartland of southern Mesopotamia produced the world's first cities by irrigating wheat and barley with Tigris and Euphrates water. By around 2300 BCE, tablets begin recording yields collapsing and complaints that "the earth turned white." The white was salt.

Irrigation in arid soils raises the water table. Evaporation pulls dissolved salts upward. Without adequate drainage and fallowing, fields salinize: wheat cannot tolerate the rising salinity, barley copes longer, but eventually nothing grows. Yields in southern Mesopotamia fell by perhaps two-thirds between 2400 and 1700 BCE; the population centre shifted northward to Babylonia. Thorkild Jacobsen and Robert McCormick Adams's 1958 paper laid out the hydrology and the archaeology in tandem.

The Mesopotamian case is foundational for environmental historians because it shows agricultural ingenuity and ecological self-undermining intertwined. The same canal networks that produced the world's first urban civilisation also poisoned its breadbasket within a millennium. Modern over-irrigated zones — the Aral Basin, parts of California and Pakistan — repeat the same pattern with bigger pumps.

concepts.title: Roman Lead, Maya Drought
concepts.contentHtml:
Greenland ice cores record a remarkable spike in atmospheric lead beginning around 500 BCE and peaking under the Roman Empire — concentrations rose roughly fourfold above pre-Phoenician background. The cause was Roman silver-smelting in Spain (Rio Tinto, Cartagena) and across the Mediterranean. Lead is a by-product of cupellation. Roman pollution was the first hemispheric-scale industrial signature, recorded in ice 4,000 km from its source.

The collapse of Classic Maya civilisation (~750–950 CE) has long puzzled archaeologists. Speleothem records from Yok Balum cave (Belize) and lake sediments (Chichancanab, Punta Laguna) now show a series of severe multi-decadal droughts coinciding with city abandonments. Douglas Kennett and colleagues argued in 2012 that drought is necessary but not sufficient — population pressure, soil exhaustion from intensive agriculture, and political fragmentation amplified climatic stress into civilisational collapse.

Both cases illustrate multicausality: environmental forcing matters, but it acts through political and economic structures. "Climate caused it" is rarely a complete story; nor is "politics caused it."

concepts.title: Easter Island Revisited
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) was the canonical morality tale: a Polynesian society that overshot its forest carrying capacity, deforested the island for moai-rolling logs, collapsed into starvation and warfare, and left only stone heads as memorial. Jared Diamond's Collapse (2005) made the story famous as ecological self-destruction.

The story is now substantially revised. Archaeological work by Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo showed that Polynesian rats (introduced by the original settlers around 1200 CE) ate palm seeds at scale, which alone could explain forest loss. Genetic and skeletal evidence suggests the Rapa Nui population was stable, not collapsing, until European contact in 1722. Then came smallpox, slave raids (Peru, 1862), and the actual demographic catastrophe.

The revised Rapa Nui story is methodologically critical. The original "ecocide" narrative read the present back into the past, casting indigenous peoples as the architects of their own ruin in ways that conveniently echoed colonial guilt-deflection. Better evidence reveals a different story: a society that managed a difficult environment for five centuries, then was destroyed by external violence and disease. The lesson is that environmental history must check its plot devices.

title: The Columbian Exchange
description: 1492 as a biological event: Crosby, plagues, and ghost acres

concepts.title: Crosby's Reframing
concepts.contentHtml:
Alfred W. Crosby's The Columbian Exchange (1972) was rejected by every major university press before Greenwood took it. Within a generation it had reshaped the discipline. Crosby's claim was simple and audacious: 1492 was less a political-military event than a biological one. Two ecosystems separated for tens of millions of years collided — and the Old World's biota largely won.

Going east-to-west: smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus, malaria, yellow fever, cattle, pigs, horses, sheep, wheat, sugar, rice, bananas, honeybees, earthworms, dandelions. Going west-to-east: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, manioc, cacao, tobacco, peppers, beans, peanuts, vanilla, syphilis (probably). Old World pathogens devastated New World populations; New World crops fed Old World population booms.

Crosby's Ecological Imperialism (1986) extended the argument: Europeans succeeded in temperate "Neo-Europes" (North America, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand) not primarily through technology but through portmanteau biota — the cattle, weeds, pathogens, and grasses that arrived with them and outcompeted local species. The conquistadors were the visible vanguard of an invisible ecological invasion.

concepts.title: The Great Dying
concepts.contentHtml:
Pre-contact population estimates for the Americas range from 50 to 100 million. By 1600, perhaps 90% of indigenous people were dead. The proximate cause was epidemiological: virgin-soil populations encountered smallpox, measles, and influenza without immunological history, and waves of pandemic spread faster than colonisers could.

Specific events stagger the imagination. Smallpox arrived in Hispaniola in 1518, in Tenochtitlan in 1520 (months before Cortés's 1521 siege), in the Inca empire by 1525 (killing Huayna Capac and triggering the succession war Pizarro exploited). The Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún recorded the testimony of Mexica survivors. Estimates by historical demographers (Cook, Borah, Henige, Denevan) vary, but the order of magnitude is settled.

The Lewis-Maslin Orbis Spike argument depends on this depopulation: roughly 56 million dead between 1492 and 1610, abandoned cropland reforesting, atmospheric CO₂ falling 7–10 ppm by 1610. The deaths were so vast they cooled the planet — visible in ice cores and tree rings as the deepest cold snap of the Little Ice Age.

concepts.title: Sugar, Slavery, and Ghost Acres
concepts.contentHtml:
The Columbian Exchange enabled the Atlantic sugar economy. Sugarcane (originally from New Guinea, refined through medieval Mediterranean and Atlantic island plantations) found ideal conditions in Brazil and the Caribbean. African labourers, forcibly transplanted by the slave trade, replaced the dying indigenous population. Madeira, São Tomé, Barbados, Jamaica, and Saint-Domingue became sugar islands. Roughly 12.5 million Africans were embarked into the Middle Passage; perhaps 2 million died at sea.

Historian Kenneth Pomeranz, in The Great Divergence (2000), argued that Britain's industrial takeoff depended on "ghost acres" — colonial land producing food, fiber, and fuel that Britain could not have grown at home. Sugar provided cheap calories for workers; cotton from American plantations fed Lancashire mills; timber and hemp from the Baltic powered the navy. Pomeranz's argument resituates British industrialisation as ecologically subsidised by the rest of the world.

This is environmental history in its most political mode: the modern world economy is not an emergent property of European cleverness, but a system that converts colonised ecosystems and enslaved labour into metropolitan wealth. The biota travelled with the ships, and the bookkeeping followed.

title: Climate and Collapse
description: Bronze Age, Late Antique, and Little Ice Age crises

concepts.title: The 4.2 Kiloyear Event and Bronze Age Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 2200 BCE, a centuries-long drought struck a swath of the Northern Hemisphere from Mesopotamia to the Indus. Speleothems, lake cores, and pollen sequences agree on the timing — geologists call it the 4.2 kiloyear event, and the ICS used it to formally define the start of the Meghalayan Age in 2018. The Akkadian Empire fell. Old Kingdom Egypt fragmented into the First Intermediate Period. The Indus Valley civilisation began its long decline. Liangzhu in China collapsed.

Whether the climate event caused these collapses or merely coincided with them remains debated. Harvey Weiss's 1993 Science paper on Tell Leilan in Syria argued for direct climatic causation. Critics noted that not every society in the affected region collapsed: southern Mesopotamia soon saw the Ur III state flourish. The pattern environmental historians now favour: climate stress is a multiplier of pre-existing political fragility, not a deterministic trigger.

A second Late Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE involved drought, earthquakes, mass migrations (the "Sea Peoples"), and the simultaneous end of the Hittite, Mycenaean, and Ugaritic civilisations. Eric Cline's 1177 BC (2014) argues for systems-collapse: many causes, mutually reinforcing, no single trigger.

concepts.title: Harper, Plague, and the End of Rome
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical historians long debated why Rome fell. Edward Gibbon (1776) blamed Christianity and barbarians. Twentieth-century revisionists emphasised slow internal transformation. Kyle Harper's The Fate of Rome (2017) put climate and disease back at the centre of the story.

The Roman Climate Optimum (~200 BCE–150 CE) gave the Empire warm, wet, stable weather coincident with its expansion. Then came cooling, drought, and three pandemics. The Antonine Plague (165–180 CE, probably smallpox) killed perhaps 10% of the empire. The Plague of Cyprian (249–262 CE) struck during the Crisis of the Third Century. The Justinianic Plague (541–549 CE, plus subsequent waves to 750 CE) was the first recorded Yersinia pestis pandemic and gutted the Eastern Roman Empire.

Tree-ring and ice-core data show a Late Antique Little Ice Age beginning with the volcanic dust veil of 536 CE, when chroniclers across Eurasia reported a year without summer. The Justinianic Plague erupted into the cooling. Harper's case: Rome was undone less by Germans than by germs and climate, with the political system overwhelmed by ecological shocks it could not buffer.

concepts.title: The Little Ice Age and the General Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
From roughly 1300 to 1850, much of the Northern Hemisphere experienced the Little Ice Age — a period of cooler temperatures, expanded glaciers, and disrupted agriculture, attributed to a combination of solar minima (Maunder, Spörer, Dalton), increased volcanism, and the post-1492 reforestation drawdown.

The seventeenth century was the worst stretch. Historian Geoffrey Parker's Global Crisis (2013), drawing on tree-ring and historical records, documented a planetary General Crisis: the Thirty Years' War in Europe, the collapse of the Ming dynasty in 1644, civil wars in England, France, the Mughal Empire, and the Ottoman state, famines from Scotland to Japan. Parker estimates perhaps a third of the human population died during the seventeenth century — a demographic catastrophe rivalling the Black Death.

His argument: climatic deterioration shortened growing seasons, raised food prices, sharpened state-society tensions everywhere. States with adaptive capacity (Tokugawa Japan) weathered it; states with rigid extraction (Ming China, Stuart England) cracked. Climate didn't write history, but it set the stress conditions under which existing political fault lines opened. The Little Ice Age is environmental history's strongest case for climate as a global historical actor.

title: Industrial Pollution
description: Coal smoke, burning rivers, and the disasters that built regulation

concepts.title: London Fog and the Birth of Air Quality Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Coal smoke had darkened London since at least the thirteenth century — Edward I issued a (largely ignored) ban in 1306. By the Victorian era, soft bituminous coal heated millions of homes, and London's winter "pea-soupers" became famous in literature and infamous in mortality statistics.

The Great Smog of December 1952 killed an estimated 4,000 to 12,000 Londoners over five days when an anticyclone trapped sulfur dioxide and particulates near ground level. Visibility fell to a few metres; cattle suffocated at Smithfield market; prison inmates choked in their cells. The toll forced the British state to act after centuries of inaction. The Clean Air Act 1956 created smoke-control areas, restricted coal burning in cities, and became a template for later environmental legislation worldwide.

The pattern would repeat across the industrial world: a visible disaster catalyses regulation that activists and scientists had been demanding for decades. London's smog also exemplifies the temporal lag between industrial onset (centuries earlier) and meaningful response. Ecological harms accumulate quietly; policy moves only after spectacle.

concepts.title: Cuyahoga, Bhopal, Chernobyl
concepts.contentHtml:
On 22 June 1969, the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland caught fire — at least the thirteenth time it had done so since 1868. Time magazine ran the story (with a photo from a 1952 fire) and the image of a burning river entered American politics. The 1970 Clean Air Act, the 1972 Clean Water Act, and the formation of the EPA followed within three years. The Cuyahoga had been so polluted by oil and industrial waste that fish couldn't survive in it; the fire was less an event than a metaphor made literal.

The night of 2–3 December 1984, a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India released about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate gas. Estimates of immediate deaths range from 3,800 (official) to 8,000+ (independent); long-term deaths from exposure exceed 20,000. The site remains contaminated four decades later. Bhopal became the defining case study in how regulatory failure, corporate cost-cutting, and the global geography of hazardous industries produce disasters in the Global South.

On 26 April 1986, reactor 4 at the Chernobyl nuclear plant exploded during a botched safety test. The exclusion zone covers 2,600 km² and remains uninhabited. The disaster accelerated glasnost, undermined Soviet legitimacy, and reshaped the global nuclear industry. Environmental historians read these three events together as the iconic disasters of late industrial modernity.

concepts.title: Minamata and the Toxic Body
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 1930s through 1968, the Chisso Corporation discharged methylmercury-contaminated wastewater into Minamata Bay in southwestern Japan. Local fish concentrated the mercury through bioaccumulation; villagers who ate the fish — and especially fetuses in utero — developed the neurological syndrome later named Minamata disease: ataxia, sensory loss, tunnel vision, congenital cerebral palsy. Cats went mad and threw themselves into the sea. Children were born with profound disabilities.

Chisso denied responsibility for years. A formal causal link was established in 1968. Litigation continued into the 1990s. W. Eugene Smith's photo essay (Life, 1972) — particularly the image "Tomoko Uemura in Her Bath" — made Minamata internationally famous as the human face of industrial poisoning.

Minamata changed environmental thought. It demonstrated bioaccumulation and biomagnification through food webs. It established that industrial pollutants enter human bodies — not as abstract threats but as embodied disability. It contributed to the 2013 Minamata Convention on Mercury, a binding international treaty. And it inaugurated a body of environmental thought (Ulrich Beck's Risk Society, Stacy Alaimo's Bodily Natures) that treats the contaminated body as the new common ground of modern ecology.

title: Conservation and Its Discontents
description: Muir, Pinchot, parks, dispossession, and Silent Spring

concepts.title: Muir Versus Pinchot
concepts.contentHtml:
The American conservation movement emerged around two men with incompatible visions. John Muir (1838–1914), Scottish-American naturalist and founder of the Sierra Club, advocated preservationism: wild nature has intrinsic value and should be protected from human use. Yosemite was his cathedral; the divine spoke through granite and sequoia.

Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946), first chief of the U.S. Forest Service under Theodore Roosevelt, championed conservation in the technocratic sense: scientific management of natural resources for maximum sustained yield. Pinchot saw forests as renewable timber stocks to be expertly harvested, not shrines to be venerated.

Their split became public over the Hetch Hetchy Valley, a Yosemite-class glacial valley approved for damming in 1913 (the dam was completed in 1923) to supply San Francisco's water. Muir fought it bitterly and died (some said) of grief. Pinchot supported it as the rational allocation of a public resource. The two philosophies still structure American environmentalism: wilderness preservation versus utilitarian management. Most actual policy is an unstable compromise between them.

concepts.title: The National Park as Erasure
concepts.contentHtml:
Yellowstone, established 1872, was the world's first national park. It was also actively cleared of its indigenous inhabitants. The Crow, Bannock, Shoshone, and Blackfeet peoples who had hunted, fished, and managed the landscape with controlled burns for millennia were excluded by treaty, force, and starvation. The U.S. Cavalry administered the park from 1886 to 1918, partly to keep "Indians" out.

The pattern repeated globally. Mark Dowie's Conservation Refugees (2009) estimates that conservation has displaced 10–20 million people worldwide, often violently. Yosemite expelled the Ahwahneechee. Glacier National Park excluded the Blackfeet. Colonial-era parks across Africa (Serengeti, Kruger) and Asia (Project Tiger reserves in India) followed the same script: cast indigenous land use as poaching, evict the inhabitants, declare the result "wilderness."

The historian Karl Jacoby's Crimes Against Nature (2001) showed that early American conservation criminalised subsistence hunting, fishing, and gathering by rural and indigenous people while protecting the recreational interests of urban elites. The wilderness ideal turned out to be a class project. "Protected" landscapes are not innocent of history; they were made through dispossession.

concepts.title: Silent Spring and the New Environmentalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) opened with a fable: a town where the birds had stopped singing because synthetic pesticides — DDT, dieldrin, parathion — had killed them, contaminated the food web, and reached human bodies. Carson's case was meticulously sourced and powerfully written. The chemical industry attacked her viciously; she was dying of breast cancer as she defended the book.

The political consequences were enormous. DDT was banned in the U.S. in 1972. The EPA was created in 1970. Silent Spring is now usually credited as the founding document of modern environmentalism — distinct from Muir's wilderness preservation and Pinchot's resource management. Carson's framing was different: the human body was already part of the contaminated ecosystem. There was no "out there" to protect from. We were inside the problem.

This shift restructured environmental politics. Toxics, public health, and environmental justice replaced wilderness as the field's centre of gravity. The 1970 Earth Day, the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act (1973), and CITES (1973) all drew on the new framing. Silent Spring didn't invent ecology, but it taught a global public that ecology was about them.

title: Climate Science and Its Politics
description: Keeling, IPCC, Kyoto, Paris, and the denial industry

concepts.title: From Arrhenius to Keeling
concepts.contentHtml:
The greenhouse effect was identified in the 1820s by Joseph Fourier. Svante Arrhenius in 1896 calculated that doubling atmospheric CO₂ would warm Earth by several degrees Celsius — a number remarkably close to modern estimates. The science sat dormant for half a century, dismissed as too slow to matter and overwhelmed by ocean uptake.

In 1958, geochemist Charles David Keeling began continuous CO₂ measurements at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. The resulting Keeling Curve showed atmospheric CO₂ rising relentlessly: 315 ppm in 1958, 350 ppm in 1988, 400 ppm in 2013, and over 425 ppm in the 2020s. The annual sawtooth (Northern Hemisphere uptake in summer, release in winter) appears as the planet's metabolism on display.

Keeling's curve transformed climate science from theoretical concern to empirical alarm. By the 1970s, modellers were projecting future warming with increasing confidence. The 1979 Charney Report, an early National Academy of Sciences synthesis, estimated climate sensitivity (warming per CO₂ doubling) at 1.5–4.5 °C, a range that barely changed for four decades until the IPCC's 2021 report narrowed it to 2.5–4 °C. The basic facts were established before today's policymakers were born.

concepts.title: The IPCC and the Treaty Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was established in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP. It does not conduct original research; it synthesises the published literature into Assessment Reports issued every 5–7 years. The First Assessment Report (1990) underpinned the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change at Rio. The Sixth Assessment (2021–23) declared anthropogenic warming "unequivocal."

The treaty cycle has produced repeated grand bargains and slow disappointments. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) bound only Annex I (developed) countries; the U.S. signed but never ratified, Canada withdrew, China and India had no targets. Emissions kept rising. The Copenhagen Summit (2009) collapsed without binding outcomes.

The Paris Agreement (2015) reframed the architecture: every country submits its own "Nationally Determined Contribution" (NDC) and ratchets ambition upward. The legally binding part is the procedure, not the targets. As of 2026, current NDCs collectively put the world on roughly a 2.5–3 °C trajectory, well above the 1.5 °C aspiration. The diplomatic process keeps moving; emissions outrun it.

concepts.title: Manufactured Doubt
concepts.contentHtml:
Through the late 1980s and 1990s, a coordinated campaign by fossil-fuel interests and allied think tanks worked to delay climate action by manufacturing public doubt about the science. Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway's Merchants of Doubt (2010), drawing on internal industry documents, traced the strategy from the tobacco industry's earlier playbook: hire contrarian scientists, fund "sound science" institutes, demand impossible certainty, target journalists with the false-balance framing.

Internal documents from Exxon (later ExxonMobil) showed the company's own scientists confirming anthropogenic warming as early as the late 1970s, while the corporation publicly funded denial through groups like the Global Climate Coalition (1989–2002). The historian Benjamin Franta has documented similar internal-knowledge-versus-public-denial patterns at Shell, BP, and the American Petroleum Institute.

The denial industry succeeded for decades. By the 2010s, public consensus was rebuilding — partly because the physical evidence (wildfires, heatwaves, hurricane intensification) became impossible to dismiss. Environmental historians now treat manufactured-doubt campaigns as a distinct genre worth studying alongside denialism about tobacco harms, ozone depletion, acid rain, and asbestos.

title: Environmental Justice
description: Warren County, Flint, Cancer Alley, and climate refugees

concepts.title: Warren County and the Birth of Environmental Justice
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1982, the state of North Carolina chose Warren County — majority Black, the poorest county in the state — to dump 60,000 tonnes of soil contaminated with PCBs. Six weeks of nonviolent protest followed. More than 500 people were arrested, including the civil-rights leader Benjamin Chavis, who coined the term environmental racism. The protest failed to stop the landfill but launched a movement.

A 1987 study by the United Church of Christ Commission for Racial Justice — Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States — found that race was the single best statistical predictor of where commercial hazardous waste facilities were sited in America, controlling for income. The 1990 University of Michigan/EPA study confirmed disparate exposure to air pollution. Environmental burdens fall hardest on communities of colour and the poor; environmental amenities (parks, clean air, tree canopy) flow toward the wealthy and white.

The 1991 First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit drafted the 17 Principles of Environmental Justice, still the movement's foundational text. Mainstream environmentalism (largely white, middle-class) was forced to reckon with its own demographic narrowness. Sociologist Robert Bullard's Dumping in Dixie (1990) became the field's first canonical text.

concepts.title: Flint and Cancer Alley
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 2014, the city of Flint, Michigan, under a state-appointed emergency manager, switched its water supply from Detroit's Lake Huron source to the Flint River to save money. Anti-corrosion treatment was skipped. Lead leached from old service lines into the drinking water of a majority-Black, low-income city of 100,000. Children's blood lead levels doubled. Officials denied the problem for eighteen months. The pediatrician Mona Hanna-Attisha forced public attention with hospital data in September 2015.

Flint became the canonical case of environmental injustice in the twenty-first century: a Black city, deprived of democratic governance, harmed by deliberate cost-cutting that would not have occurred in a white middle-class city. Lead exposure causes irreversible cognitive damage. The demographic legacy will persist for decades.

Cancer Alley — an 85-mile stretch along the Mississippi between Baton Rouge and New Orleans — hosts more than 150 petrochemical plants and refineries, sited overwhelmingly on the lands of historic Black communities, many descended from freedpeople. EPA modelling put the estimated cancer risk from air toxics at up to about 50 times the national average in some census tracts. The historian Barbara Allen's Uneasy Alchemy (2003) documented how zoning, plant siting, and political marginalisation combined to produce one of the densest petrochemical landscapes on Earth.

concepts.title: Climate Refugees and Loss-and-Damage
concepts.contentHtml:
Environmental injustice scales globally. The countries that contributed least to historical greenhouse-gas emissions — Bangladesh, Pacific Island states (Tuvalu, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands), the Sahel, low-elevation coastal Africa — face the worst climate impacts. The wealthy industrial nations that built their prosperity on fossil carbon are largely insulated by money and geography from the consequences they triggered.

The figure of the climate refugee entered international discourse in the 1990s and remains contested in international law. The 1951 Refugee Convention does not recognise climate as a basis for protection; the 2018 Global Compact for Migration is non-binding. Estimates of climate-driven displacement by 2050 range widely (the World Bank's Groundswell report estimates 216 million internal migrants by 2050) but agree on the direction: tens to hundreds of millions, mostly internal, mostly poor.

The 2022 COP27 at Sharm el-Sheikh established a Loss and Damage fund — the first formal acknowledgment that wealthy emitters owe compensation to poorer countries for irrecoverable climate harms. The fund's actual operationalisation has been slow, contested, and underfunded. But the principle — that climate harm is unjustly distributed and demands restitution — is now part of the diplomatic vocabulary.

title: Decolonising Environmental History
description: Indigenous knowledge, planetary commons, and Chakrabarty's species-history

concepts.title: Indigenous Knowledge as Environmental Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of its existence, environmental history was written by people educated in European universities using European archives. Indigenous environmental knowledge — accumulated over millennia, encoded in language, ritual, and land practice — was largely treated as folklore rather than data. That has changed.

Aboriginal Australian fire management, which shaped Australian biota over 60,000 years, is now studied seriously by ecologists and increasingly applied through programmes like the Northern Territory's savanna burning. Bill Gammage's The Biggest Estate on Earth (2011) reframed the Australian continent as deliberately managed, not a wilderness Europeans "discovered." North American work by Robin Wall Kimmerer (Braiding Sweetgrass, 2013) and historian Lisa Brooks (Our Beloved Kin, 2018) returns indigenous epistemologies to the centre of environmental thought.

The Amazon, long described in school textbooks as virgin rainforest, is being recognised as a heavily human-shaped ecosystem. Pre-Columbian Amazonian peoples engineered terra preta soils, domesticated dozens of species (including cassava, peach palm, possibly cacao), and maintained agroforestry systems whose scale archaeologists are still mapping with LiDAR. The forest the Spaniards saw was not pristine — it was a 5,000-year-old garden.

concepts.title: The Planetary Commons
concepts.contentHtml:
Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990, Nobel 2009) overturned Garrett Hardin's "tragedy of the commons" by documenting many real-world commons that had been sustainably managed for centuries by communities with the right institutional design. Ostrom's eight design principles — clear boundaries, locally appropriate rules, collective-choice arrangements, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict-resolution, recognition by authorities, nested enterprises — became the empirical foundation for thinking about shared resources.

The planetary commons framing extends Ostrom upward. The atmosphere, the oceans, biodiversity, the cryosphere, and global biogeochemical cycles are commons in the strict sense: rivalrous (one country's emissions reduce the carbon budget for others) and non-excludable (no one can be kept out of the climate system).

The planetary boundaries framework, articulated by Johan Rockström and colleagues in 2009, identifies nine such commons — climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, atmospheric aerosols, ozone, novel entities — with thresholds beyond which Earth-system stability cannot be assumed. A 2023 assessment found six of the nine transgressed, and a 2025 update added ocean acidification as a seventh. The framework has become foundational for environmental governance debates.

concepts.title: Chakrabarty's Species-History
concepts.contentHtml:
The Indian historian Dipesh Chakrabarty's essay "The Climate of History: Four Theses" (Critical Inquiry, 2009) is now the most-cited theoretical contribution to Anthropocene scholarship. Chakrabarty's central provocation: anthropogenic climate change collapses the modern distinction between natural history (deep, slow, geological) and human history (recent, contingent, political). Humans have become a geological force. The historian must now write at species and planetary scales, not merely at the scale of nations or classes.

This is uncomfortable for several traditions. Marxism wants capital, not "humanity," to bear responsibility — and Chakrabarty agrees that capital is the proximate cause but argues species-level framing is also necessary, since the consequences fall on Homo sapiens regardless of class. Postcolonial theory worries about "we humans" framings that erase historical responsibility for emissions. Chakrabarty's later work (The Climate of History in a Planetary Age, 2021) tries to hold both scales — the unequal political causes and the universal biospheric consequences — simultaneously.

The result is a discipline being remade. Environmental history of the 2020s is global, multi-scalar, methodologically eclectic, and politically aware that it is not just describing the past but writing the prologue to whatever comes next.
